articles.title_orig: China's Communist Party Tightens Oversight of Officials
articles.title_zh: China's Communist Party Tightens Oversight of Officials
articles.content_orig:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

articles.title_orig: No homosexual offence disregards since law introduced in Northern Ireland
articles.title_zh: No homosexual offence disregards since law introduced in Northern Ireland
articles.content_orig:
There have been no pardons for convictions for now abolished gay sex offences in the eight years since a scheme was introduced in Northern Ireland.
Three people have applied to the pardons and disregards scheme since the laws introduction , however their applications did not meet the relevant criteria.
Offences include gross indecency and procuring others to commit homosexual acts. The activity must have been consensual, with a person aged 17 or over and must not still be an offence.
The Department of Justice (DoJ) said a review of the scope of the scheme is taking place, with a view to making reform proposals to ministers after the next assembly elections.
The scheme was approved by the Northern Ireland Assembly in 2016 and came into force in 2018.
Posthumous pardons automatically apply to anyone convicted of offences who have since died.
While a definitive number of those convicted has not been formally established, it is estimated that hundreds can apply .
Male homosexual acts were criminalised until 1982 in Northern Ireland.
The Rainbow Project helped some of those who applied for their conviction to be quashed or disregarded.
The charity's chief executive, Scott Cuthbertson, said he is not surprised at the low uptake, but "that doesn't mean the scheme hasn't been a success".
"There's the message it sends that what happened prior to 1982 was wrong and shouldn't have happened and that the people who were convicted under legislation at that point deserve not to have that stain on their record," he said.
"When it comes to the low uptake, I would encourage anyone who has that on their record, who wants to remove it and are maybe a wee bit worried about opening up old wounds or dealing with past issues, it is worth it."
Cuthbertson also welcomed the DoJ's review.
"I think anything that can be done to make people aware of the scheme and increase the uptake of the number of people applying would be a good idea."
Jeffrey Dudgeon, a gay rights campaigner, won a landmark legal case in the European Court which ruled that the law was in breach of the human right to a private life .
He told BBC News NI that he "always knew that there wouldn't be very many people eligible for pardons given the length of time had elapsed since".
"I would say most of the people involved in that had either died or were not really interested in in resurrecting the whole matter."
He said there was a "different mood" in the preceding years before decriminalisation.
"From the late '60s until 1982, which is the period I was mostly involved in, gay liberation had happened in America and in England. The whole mood had changed from being a sort of  silent minority that was pleading for decriminalisation and we'd become an organised group looking for rights.
"The big problem always was that most convictions were not exactly within the remit or ambit of the criminal law that was repealed in 1982. Which was very particular in that it was only decriminalised gay sex between men over 21 in private.
"I think a lot of the actual cases that came into the courts involved some form of sex with somebody under 21 or in public or was it with a third party present."
Prof Tom Hulme is a cultural historian of modern Ireland and Britain at Queen's University Belfast.
He said that the history of same sex convictions in Northern Ireland is "quite a complex one" as Victorian laws were used against gay and bisexual men prior to decriminalisation.
After the repeal in 1982, laws against acts such as sex in public places, which remain illegal today, were used disproportionately against gay and bisexual men, due to attitudes towards homosexual activity in Northern Ireland, he said.
"Far more people were arrested throughout Northern Ireland than had been in the previous hundred or so years, so there is an issue here with convictions in that the repeal scheme or the disregard scheme that is in current existence essentially does not capture many of those offences because they are still in essence illegal today.
"You have to remember that these were not people convicted as such for being homosexual or gay or bisexual but they were rather convicted for acts that had taken place in public places."
Hulme said that there needs to be a "broader public conversation about the conditions under which gay men and bisexual men were seeking sex" and the role of the police during these times.
"There is much more to learn about Northern Ireland's gay and bisexual history and that might provide some form of redress as well."
In England and Wales, the scheme was initially open to men with specific convictions for homosexual offences that have since been repealed.
It was extended in June 2023 with the aim to enable more people, including women and those serving in the UK armed forces, to apply.
Since then, 19 convictions have been eligible for a disregard for the year ending March 2026, lower than the 35 convictions in the previous year.
Prior to the extended scheme, there were 522 applicants and 208 convictions were eligible for a disregard.
In Scotland, 22 people have applied to have their convictions disregarded and 16 applications have been granted since 2019.
The legislation provides an automatic pardon for any man convicted of same-sex activity between men that would be legal today.

articles.title_orig: Bond investors sit out ‘most consequential’ US midterm elections in years
articles.title_zh: Bond investors sit out ‘most consequential’ US midterm elections in years
articles.content_orig:
Investors expect a blue wave in next week's midterm election , as Democrats surge in polls and President Donald Trump 's approval rating remains low.
Public polling suggests Democrats are likely to take control of the House of Representatives, and analysts who parse what politics means for investors are in overdrive to tell their clients how to prepare for what Congress will look like after the Tuesday election.
Concern about the spending plans and priorities of a Democratic-controlled Congress permeates analyst reports reviewed by CNBC. But because Trump has another two years of his presidency, a divided government would likely create gridlock that would prevent congressional leadership in opposition to the president from getting much done, analysts are advising their clients.
Most analysts believe Democrats are also within striking distance of a Senate majority, though that outcome is significantly less likely than a House flip according to the polls. Next Tuesday's elections will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress for the remainder of Trump's presidency, after two years of full Republican control.
Divided government typically makes must-pass legislation, like government funding and raising the debt ceiling , harder to enact. A debt ceiling standoff — or first-ever default on federal debt — could be particularly damaging.
Wall Street watchers are also expecting Democrats to try to advance an ambitious and expensive agenda should they gain control of Congress. An Oct. 29 report from Piper Sandler analyzing Congressional Budget Office data projected that policy proposals from Democrats "would add $5 trillion to the deficit over the coming decade." The analysis assumes repeals of Trump's tariffs and reversing cuts to Medicaid, nutrition programs and Affordable Care Act subsidies.
Major policy swings — and big spending packages — become less likely as a divided government is unlikely to agree on issues. That's a dynamic the market typically enjoys. Trump's veto power would effectively block major Democratic policies from becoming law.
"A blue House is the obvious consensus base case," Wolfe Research said in an Oct. 27 report. The firm surveyed 138 investors and found 96% of those polled believed Democrats would prevail in House control.
"The scale of polling error that would be required for Republicans to retain House control would be unprecedented in modern history, well above the polling error in the famously bad 2020 cycle," Wolfe wrote.
Wolfe is less bullish on a Democratic Senate, though investors clearly see a possibility that Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress.
Fifty-eight percent of investors the firm surveyed believed Democrats would gain control of the Senate, while 42% believed Republicans would retain control of the chamber. The investors surveyed were more bullish than Wolfe itself, which puts the chances of a Democratic Senate at 49%.
Other analysts are largely coalescing around the potential for a good night for Democrats.
"A blue wave scenario has become our base case," an Oct. 20 report from TD Securities reads. An Oct. 23 Raymond James report says "Democrats are in a solid position to win a majority in the House of Representatives and are increasingly likely to win enough seats to capture a Senate majority."
Even if Democrats sweep both chambers, protracted battles could still play out as Republicans maintain the White House and the Senate must still surpass the 60-vote filibuster threshold.
Democrats winning control of the Senate could allay concerns about the Federal Reserve's independence from Trump, TD predicted.
That's because any new Fed members would need to be confirmed by the Senate, which would be unlikely to support a nominee who wouldn't support the central bank charting its own course.
Democrats are also expected to investigate companies that have done business with the Trump administration should they win control of a chamber. The majority party in Congress holds subpoena power on committees. Some Democrats have already telegraphed their investigative priorities ahead of the election.
The debt ceiling is likely the most critical sticking point for the economy that lawmakers will need to address during the next Congress, unless Republicans raise it during the lame-duck session between the election and the start of the next Congress in January. The Bipartisan Policy Center expects the U.S. will reach the debt limit between late-winter and mid-summer 2027.
"While negotiations around the debt ceiling may come down to the wire, a Democratic Congress would make it slightly more likely that a bill is passed than a divided Congress," TD said.
If Congress does not raise the debt ceiling, the U.S. could default on its debt, causing catastrophic economic consequences.
Democrats, should they control one slice of government, are expected to demand concessions from Republicans in exchange for their votes to raise the debt ceiling. That sets up a potential standoff, which analysts note Republicans could avoid if they lose next week and raise the debt ceiling during the lame duck.
"[R]aising the debt limit before January could substantially reduce leverage Democrats have over healthcare, Medicaid, SNAP, and broader domestic spending priorities in the next Congress," Raymond James told its clients.
Correction: This story has been corrected to reflect that the Bipartisan Policy Center projects the U.S. will reach its debt limit next year. An earlier version mischaracterized the center's projection.

articles.title_orig: Military briefing: what would another US-Iran conflict look like?
articles.title_zh: Military briefing: what would another US-Iran conflict look like?
articles.content_orig:
Israel could unleash a devastating surprise attack targeting Iran's top military leaders if war resumes after Tuesday's midterm elections, potentially employing tactics similar to its sophisticated 2024 operation that crippled Hezbollah, the New York Post reported Saturday.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier is reportedly heading to the Middle East to join the USS George Washington and USS George W. Bush as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military action against Tehran.
Trump told Kansas City radio station KCMO Friday that the conflict is "going to get wrapped up soon," although he did not elaborate.
Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., predicted military action could come immediately after the elections.
"I'm going to guess about a day or three after this election, I would not want to be anywhere close to Iran," Marshall said Thursday.
Former Mossad Deputy Head of Global Operations Oded Ailam told the outlet that Israel could execute another operation resembling its extraordinary September 2024 pager attack against Hezbollah, this time targeting four Iranian military hard-liners believed to exercise effective control over the regime.
"This is the bread and butter of Israeli strategy, is surprise twists and turns, unexpected moves and I'm absolutely certain that Israel has cards in the sleeve that will be used," Ailam said.
The 2024 operation was among the most creative, planned and devastating intelligence attacks in modern warfare.
On Sept. 17-18, thousands of explosive-rigged pagers and walkie-talkies used by Hezbollah operatives detonated across Lebanon and Syria, killing dozens, injuring thousands and severely disrupting the Iranian-backed terrorist organization's communications.
The meticulously coordinated attack required years of planning, sophisticated intelligence gathering, and infiltration of Hezbollah's communications supply chain, demonstrating Israel's extraordinary ability to identify, penetrate, and strike its enemies from within.
That precedent raises the possibility that Israeli intelligence already knows the identities, movements, and vulnerabilities of Iran's military leadership and has spent years preparing similarly unexpected operations.
According to Ailam, Iran's real power rests with four military figures: Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander Ahmad Vahidi, Basij commander Hossein Taeb, armed forces chief Ali Abdollahi and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei.
"The president and foreign minister can't make decisions. [The military junta] hides behind Mojtaba, but he's not in charge; he's a complete puppet," Ailam said, referring to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
"Israel will use its imagination, its intelligence and the ability of the Israelis to surprise and turn the table in ways you can not anticipate," he added.
Ailam said the Iranian leadership is increasingly divided over negotiations with Washington, with military hard-liners repeatedly undermining diplomatic efforts.
"They're not on the same page themselves, we see a lot of friction within the regime, different approaches, agreeing then reneging," he said.
Retired U.S. Gen. Jack Keane advocated strikes against Iran's leadership, nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure and missile and drone production capabilities.
"The intelligence we have now as a result of six months of collection during the on-again, off-again ceasefire is significant," Keane said.
Ailam suggested that another Israeli intelligence operation could inflict psychological damage exceeding that of a conventional military invasion.
"The effect is enormous, especially on the psychology of the enemy. Imagine after the attack there's a conversation somewhere in a bunker with the top echelons of Iran and everybody's looking to the left and to the right and thinking the guy next to him is a spy," he said.
However, analysts warned that renewed attacks could provoke devastating Iranian retaliation.
"[The regime's] interest is survival; they'll fight harder," said Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
Former IDF Maj. Gen. Yaakov Amidror warned that Iranian strikes against Gulf energy infrastructure could trigger an overwhelming Israeli response.
"If the Iranian retaliation will be to destroy or try to destroy energy facilities in the Gulf countries, that would be a good excuse for Israel to destroy the whole energy infrastructure in Iran," Amidror said.
"This is something that cannot be rebuilt in a few years, this will send Iran back 50 years," he added.
Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., pushed back against the Trump administration's reported military planning.
"Their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law," Murphy said Thursday.
"The plan that they have developed will lead in my view to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that in my view will be devastating for our security interests," he added.
Despite any speculation about a leadership strike, Amidror emphasized that Israel's overriding military priority remains eliminating Iran's nuclear weapons potential and ballistic missile capabilities.

articles.title_orig: Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
articles.title_zh: Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
articles.content_orig:
Bolivia has declared a nationwide state of emergency to free up resources to deal with the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.
Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz signed the decree on Saturday, which also called for further deployments of rescue teams in areas of the country hard hit by flooding and drought.
El Nino will have “very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods”, Paz said, adding that Bolivia needs “the cooperation of all institutions”.
Drought is now affecting 78,000 families in six of Bolivia’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, according to a government report this week.
Bolivia is also prone to flooding. In December 2025, floods in the Santa Cruz region killed dozens of people.
Neighbouring Chile’s capital, Santiago, recorded the rainiest October ever, while wildfires in Peru killed at least 12 people last month.
El Nino, a global climate phenomenon that occurs roughly every two to seven years, is part of the planet’s natural weather cycle.
During this climate event, warming in the Pacific Ocean brings worldwide changes in winds, pressure, and rainfall patterns, often causing extreme weather.
El Nino’s intensity varies, and its impact changes based on geographic location, but this cycle could be the strongest in recorded history . It is due to peak at the end of 2026, but its impacts could continue well into 2027.
Scientists predict El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths globally , with the poorest countries worst impacted.
In early September, the World Meteorological Organization reported a nearly 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027.

articles.title_orig: Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
articles.title_zh: Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
articles.content_orig:
Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued the UK's future should be inside the EU, and that Brexit has made the country "poorer, weaker and less secure".
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Reeves said she welcomed debate around the UK's relationship with Europe.
At the last election, Labour's manifesto said a Labour government would stay outside the EU and make Brexit work.
But Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there needs to be an honest discussion about what the future relationship looks like.
The Conservatives have said there is no desire to rerun the Brexit debate and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has said there is no mandate to pursue closer EU ties.
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Burnham has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is next due by 2029.
In the Sunday Times , Reeves wrote: "No-one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were. I do believe Britain's future lies in the European Union."
She said supporters of rejoining the EU had to "make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right".
Reeves added that at the forthcoming UK-EU summit, she hoped for confirmation of the youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for since she was in office.
She also said she was hoping for "progress towards entry" into the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme.
Announced last March, SAFE is part of an EU-wide effort to rearm after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A defence pact agreed with the EU last May paved the way for UK-based defence companies to be part of projects funded by SAFE.
In her piece for the Sunday Times, Reeves also sought to defend her record in office.
She wrote about the need for governments to be "braver" in building big infrastructure projects and "clear eyed" about the risks and benefits AI would drive in advanced economies.

articles.title_orig: Judge won't dismiss McRib class-action lawsuit against McDonald's
articles.title_zh: Judge won't dismiss McRib class-action lawsuit against McDonald's
articles.content_orig:
A 'Barron's Roundtable' panel discusses how the fast-food chain will manage the pinch on consumers' wallets.
A federal judge ruled Friday that McDonald's must face a proposed class action lawsuit accusing the fast-food giant of misleading customers about the meat used in its popular McRib sandwich.
U.S. District Judge April Perry in Chicago rejected the company's bid to dismiss the lawsuit in its entirety, allowing consumer deception, fraud and unjust enrichment claims to proceed while dismissing five other claims without prejudice.
The lawsuit, filed by four consumers in December, alleges that McDonald's designed the McRib patty to resemble a rack of pork ribs despite containing no actual rib meat.
The plaintiffs argue that the sandwich's name, appearance and marketing mislead customers into believing they are purchasing a more expensive cut of pork.
MCDONALD'S HIT WITH LAWSUIT CLAIMING MCRIB CONTAINS NO REAL RIB MEAT
McDonald's must face a proposed class action lawsuit accusing the fast-food giant of misleading customers about the meat used in its popular McRib sandwich. (David Paul Morris/Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Perry determined that it was too early to conclude that consumers could not reasonably expect the sandwich to contain rib meat, citing allegations about its marketing and consumer surveys submitted by the plaintiffs.
One survey found that 72% of respondents expected the McRib to contain rib meat, while another found that 67% considered rib meat important or very important to their purchasing decision, according to the court filing.
The ruling allows portions of the case to proceed but does not establish that McDonald's engaged in deceptive advertising.
NELSON PELTZ-LED GROUP OFFERS TO BUY WENDY’S FOR $1.4B
There are nearly 45,000 McDonald's restaurants worldwide. (Edgar Su/Reuters, File / Reuters Photos)
As FOX Business previously reported , the lawsuit alleges that the McRib contains lower-grade pork products, including pork shoulder, heart, tripe and stomach, rather than rib meat.
McDonald's has denied the allegations, maintaining that the sandwich contains 100% pork sourced from U.S. farmers and suppliers. The company previously told FOX Business that it does not use heart, tripe or scalded stomach in the McRib patty.
McDonald's argued that the sandwich's name does not mislead reasonable consumers and that its publicly available ingredient list identifies pork as the primary ingredient.
Perry rejected the argument that the McRib's trademarked name shields the company from deceptive marketing claims, noting that other McDonald's products, including the McChicken and Egg McMuffin, have names that describe their ingredients.

A representative for McDonald's did not immediately respond to FOX Business' request for comment.
Introduced in 1981, the McRib has developed a loyal following through its periodic limited-time returns to McDonald's menus. The sandwich features a boneless pork patty covered in barbecue sauce and topped with onions and pickles.
There are nearly 14,000 McDonald's restaurants in the U.S. and more than 45,000 worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Thousands rally in Israel urging ‘Jewish-Arab’ coalition to oust Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Thousands rally in Israel urging ‘Jewish-Arab’ coalition to oust Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of people have rallied in Tel Aviv to urge the Israeli opposition to make a deal with Arab parties to remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Protesters at Saturday’s rally told the AFP news agency this may be the “last chance for real change” and that Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is a “great manipulator”.
Main opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Israel’s Arab parties, but a deadlock in Tuesday’s elections means siding with the parties could help him form a government.
“People really want this vote for change to work out, and they believe that… Gadi Eisenkot and other leaders of the Jewish-Israeli parties need to listen to their voice,” Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh said from Ramallah on Saturday.
Counter-protesters also showed up to Saturday’s demonstrations, with Netanyahu supporters seen shouting their own demands that “Israel should not have a government with so-called terrorists”, Odeh said.
Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s elections, while Eisenkot’s won 48, meaning neither side can form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament alone.
Israel’s three Arab-led parties won 19 seats, having made significant gains in Tuesday’s election.
Nearly 840,000 people voted for Ra’am and the Joint List, a coalition of three Arab-led parties, a 64 percent increase from the last elections in 2022, according to the Central Election Committee.
The Arab electoral success means a coalition with Eisenkot would provide a comfortable majority of 67. However, for many in Israel, the idea of siding with Arabs is politically unpalatable.
Netanyahu has accused Palestinian-Israeli parties of “stealing” the polls and accepting funding from Qatar to do it. Qatar has rejected the allegations , calling it a disinformation campaign.
Odeh said that Israeli right-wing circles have described “the historic turnout of Palestinian Israelis as electoral terrorism, equating it to the October 7th attack”, when Hamas-led fighters stormed southern Israel, killing more than 1,200 people and taking hundreds captive.
“Palestinian-Israeli votes and voices” are under attack because they have a “prominent position” in deciding whether Eisenkot can form a government, she added.

articles.title_orig: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
articles.title_zh: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
articles.content_orig:
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.
Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
As night fell, demonstrations turned violent.
A large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed. The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing trainers and other items, local media reported.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
Poseck said: "We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Similar instances took place in other German cities, following earlier largely peaceful demonstrations.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind".
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across France to deal with the demonstrations, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 500 arrests after clashes in Toulouse, Lyon and Marseille.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail. Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

Atlus apparently can’t keep a secret.
Alleged footage of a Persona 1 Remake has emerged online, although in this age of AI generated content it’s incredibly difficult to ascertain whether this is legit or not.
My jerk reaction is that it’s probably real, as it appears to include reused animations from the unreleased Persona 4 Revival . A similar leak occurred prior to the official announcement of Persona 3 Reload .
But as always, you should take this with a pinch of salt.
The video shows combat featuring characters from Persona 1, alongside Persona 2’s protagonist Tatsuya Suou.
Series producer Kazuhisa Wada has spoken quite candidly about how Persona 1 and 2 remakes are something Atlus should “eventually do”, so this project has been an open secret for some time now.
It’s worth noting that Persona 4 Revival is due out on 17th February, so even if this footage is real, I wouldn’t expect two remakes in the same year. It’s probably still a little way away.

articles.title_orig: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
articles.title_zh: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
articles.content_orig:
When they met in northern Serbia last November, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučiċ and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán could hardly have guessed they would both be out of power within a year.
Both were ousted by popular movements - Orbán fell first, in April, defeated by Péter Magyar's Tisza party. Then last Sunday a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.
The Tisza party in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia look very different - Tisza is centred on the personality and energy of its leader, while the students in Serbia insist they have no leadership.
But the huge turnout - 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia, was driven by tech-savvy young people in both countries. They used AI tools to crunch numbers, identify threats to the vote, and mobilise tens of thousands of election monitors to prevent intimidation and electoral fraud by the governing parties.
Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.
Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.
During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.
A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.
"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."
Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.
Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.
Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.
They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.
A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.
The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.
There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force.
Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment.
An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.
There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.
Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number.
"It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC.
"The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.
Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.
Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power.
The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other.
Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement.
"There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC.
"In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

articles.title_orig: Persian Gulf scrambling to prevent Iran war from again hitting its doorstep
articles.title_zh: Persian Gulf scrambling to prevent Iran war from again hitting its doorstep
articles.content_orig:
States on the continent and in the region are building new frameworks to prevent escalation
“Anything’s possible” was Donald Trump’s response when asked if he would launch a new attack on Iran after the midterm elections. Fears of what a return to all-out war would bring have set off a flurry of diplomacy. Two noteworthy tracks from European and regional powers have emerged as last-gasp attempts to prevent, or at least limit, the destruction a renewed conflict would cause. If they succeed, they could become the pillars of a new “coalition of the willing” to stabilise the Middle East without America in the lead.
The first track brings together the E4—Britain, France, Germany and Italy—and the R4 of Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia . The foreign ministers of the E4+R4 met in Istanbul on October 23rd to discuss preserving the viability of a two-state solution in Israel-Palestine, ending the US-Iran war, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and defending Saudi Arabia against the latest offensive launched by the Houthis, a Yemeni rebel group.
On the European side, the addition of Italy to the E3 is welcome. It bolsters Europe’s diplomatic weight, offsetting Britain’s Brexit-induced weakness and Germany’s loss of regional influence over its staunch support for Israel . Berlin’s relations with Tehran have also been tense since 2022, when Iran’s human-rights abuses and its military assistance to Russia soured ties. Italy does not carry the same baggage, nor did it take part in the E3’s decision last year to trigger the “snapback” of sanctions on Iran. That could eventually help it reopen the path to negotiations.
The Istanbul meeting also showed how far the R4 has come since it formed earlier this year in response to the shifting power balance in the Middle East. All its members but Egypt signed the Mecca Defence Alliance, a military pact, in August. The pact was recently tested when members activated the collective defence measures in response to the Houthi offensive against Saudi Arabia. The grouping signals that the region’s powers are increasingly willing to take responsibility for their own security.
The second diplomatic track opened three days after the Istanbul gathering, when security chiefs from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia met Iran’s leaders in Tehran. The meeting was an attempt by regional powers to avert a new round of fighting by including Iran in a serious diplomatic process. It also allowed Iran to host, giving it a PR victory at a time when the Trump administration is attempting to impose a full blockade on the country.
These regional powers are scrambling to de-escalate as Tehran has made clear that its response to renewed US or Israeli strikes would be far more damaging than anything the Middle East has absorbed in the past eight months. It has already shown its reach through its ally in Yemen. In recent weeks the Houthis have damaged critical infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia and attacked shipping through the Red Sea. A joint effort by the Houthis and Iran to disrupt transit through two vital waterways—the straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb—would have global economic ramifications. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia probably also warned Iran during the Tehran meeting that further strikes on its neighbours’ critical infrastructure and civilian targets would undo any prospect of regional integration.
Whether these tracks succeed or fail, they point to a changing reality. Most glaring is America’s absence from both meetings, as European and regional powers increasingly try to work around an unpredictable Washington rather than with it. For the R4, the Trump administration’s handling of Iran has shattered the assumption that America’s armed forces offer iron-clad protection to its allies, a reality Europeans are also confronting over Ukraine. America and Israel might have the military capacity to devastate the region, but they have proved unable or unwilling to win the peace. Left to pick up the pieces, Middle Eastern and European countries have been made all too aware that stronger diplomatic efforts are needed for their own security.
If war and maximum pressure pushed Iran, a country of more than 90 million people, towards state collapse, the consequences for its neighbours and Europe would be disastrous. This is particularly so given that neither America nor Israel is likely to invest the time and money needed to rebuild it. Yet the Islamic Republic’s elite will probably remain in power for the foreseeable future. And as the Tehran meeting showed, the hard-line military factions that the war has brought to the fore currently dominate decision-making.
The immediate priority for both tracks is to prevent a return to high-intensity war. It remains to be seen whether the E4+R4 can exert influence over both Trump and Tehran to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. But their combined leverage, if used with greater purpose and willingness, could add new force to diplomacy.
Teaming up more actively with the R4 would also give Europe better access to Washington and Tehran, both of which have increasingly dismissed European influence. That would improve Europe’s chances of advancing two of its strategic objectives: ensuring the peaceful nature of Iran’s future nuclear programme, and stabilising the Middle East. The E4 and R4 could also use their combined economic clout to press China to use its deep trade ties with Iran to secure the lasting reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
The regional powers have also seen an advantage in fostering deeper cooperation with Europe. Relative to Russia, China and the US, Europeans can provide a more reliable partnership in security, defence and economic affairs. As the R4 countries seek to strengthen their defences, modernise their militaries and heal their economies after successive wars, Europe remains an attractive partner.
The E4 could also help middle powers in the region contain and potentially moderate the behaviour of both Israel and Iran. Europeans could restrain Israeli military activity in Lebanon and Syria through stronger economic and technical support to central governments and increased funding for the Lebanese Armed Forces. The R4 will similarly look to European countries to expand measures targeting Israeli occupation policies and illegal settlements.
On Iran, Europe and its regional partners could use the prospect of eventual sanctions relief to nudge Tehran towards a stronger agreement on its nuclear programme and reducing its destabilising conduct in the Middle East. The E4 and R4 share concerns that in a future deal with Iran, Washington may be willing to curtail the role of the International Atomic Energy Agency in monitoring Iran’s nuclear activities. Europeans could therefore make EU sanctions relief conditional on enhanced international monitoring, whatever Washington agrees bilaterally with Iran. The R4 could reinforce this by offering to be the first to invest in Iran’s post-sanctions economy, given that European companies, wary of reputational exposure, are likely to be slower to return.
Both the E4 and R4 view Iran’s missile and drone programme as a direct threat. Yet precisely because of its demonstrated effectiveness in the past year, Tehran is unlikely to negotiate a major rollback. Instead, the E4 and R4 could intensify efforts to slow Iran’s advances by disrupting supply chains from China and Russia and interdicting shipments to groups such as Hizbullah and the Houthis. They could also press Beijing to demand that Iran halt technology transfers to non-state armed actors.
The E4+R4 format creates opportunities for Europeans and regional powers to lay the foundations of a broader security architecture for the Middle East, one that goes beyond the deterrence framework envisaged by the Mecca pact. articles.title_orig: Chili’s Margaritas Rimmed With Degreaser Burn 5 People in North Carolina
articles.title_zh: Chili’s Margaritas Rimmed With Degreaser Burn 5 People in North Carolina
articles.content_orig:
FOREST CITY, N.C. -- An investigation occurred after a chemical exposure incident at a Chili's Grill & Bar in western North Carolina, officials confirmed.
The incident led to multiple people enduring chemical burns after consuming drinks that were prepared with a cleaning chemical mistakenly identified as sugar, according to a press release from the Foothills Health District. This occurred at the restaurant's Forest City location.
The Foothills Health District said preliminary information indicates that on Monday, Oct. 26, an employee received a "granulated degreasing chemical" from a contracted worker power-washing the outside of the restaurant and put it in an unlabeled container. The container was then brought into the restaurant and left in the bar area, the public health agency said.
On Wednesday, Oct. 28, an employee preparing the bar for lunch service found the container and used it to prepare margaritas, believing it was sugar.
According to the release, three customers later ordered margaritas and "immediately experienced discomfort" and had chemical burns in and around their mouths, before telling staff of the situation and leaving to seek medical attention. In response, two restaurant employees tasted the substance in the container and had similar symptoms, per preliminary findings.
"I'm not sure what degree of chemical burns they had, but they went to urgent care and were treated there," Foothills Health District spokesperson Megan Rollins said.
The Foothills Health District then opened an investigation and issued an immediate suspension of the food service permit at the Chili's location. Staff were instructed to thoroughly wash and sanitize affected food preparation areas, as well as equipment and surfaces.
Levonne Baker, a regular Chili's customer, spoke to News 13 about the incident.
SEE ALSO: McDonald's worker in CA in ICU after coworker allegedly throws hot oil, causing severe burns
"I was beyond surprised and almost scared," Baker said. He described the situation as something out of a horror movie.
"It's like a Wes Craven story that's coming to life. I mean, you don't get margaritas that can burn your skin," Baker said.
Baker says the incident has also made him reconsider whether he will return to the restaurant's bar.
"It has made me a little nervous about going back to the bar because it's like, what's in there next? I mean, am I going to be the next person who's going next door? And not for an oil change," he said.
As of Thursday morning, environmental health specialists with Foothills Health District have completed their investigation. The food service permit at the Chili's location has also been reinstated after officials determined the restaurant met "all applicable food safety requirements."
The restaurant chain was contacted for comment but had not responded at the time of the report.
Health officials say the incident highlights the importance of properly labeling chemicals in workplaces and homes to prevent accidental exposure. Rollins added that by having everything labeled, if something is still ingested, it can be easier to identify.
"Then you can call Poison Control, and they can walk you through exactly how to neutralize that chemical," Rollins said.

articles.title_orig: US plans to deport Afghans back to their home country through Pakistan, documents show
articles.title_zh: US plans to deport Afghans back to their home country through Pakistan, documents show
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan on the first flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.
The proposed deportation flight, which has not been publicly announced, could take place as early as Monday, according to rights advocates and families of detainees.
Among those facing deportation are relatives of Afghans who worked with the U.S. military in its 20-year war against the Taliban, which is now back in power. The deportees could face severe repercussions should Pakistan return them to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan as is widely expected.
Afghans driven from their country by war and political instability have been welcomed by the U.S. for decades, including tens of thousands who fled the country following the chaotic withdrawal of U.S.-led forces in 2021. President Donald Trump halted admissions for Afghans and other refugees when he returned to office last year as part of a broader immigration crackdown.
His administration has deported thousands of people to countries that are not their own, many of them in Africa , in what immigration lawyers say is an effort to skirt international laws against returning asylum-seekers to the countries they fled from. The legality of these so-called third-country deportation agreements is set to be debated by the Supreme Court in December.
It is not clear what kind of formal agreement the U.S. may have with Pakistan, but the senior administration official said the U.S. charter flight would not be able to land there without the Pakistan government’s knowledge and approval. The deportation plan was earlier reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times.
Bloomberg cited a federal government official familiar with the plans as a source for its report, while The New York Times cited three U.S. officials.
Shawn VanDiver, president of the San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said it had confirmed that in recent days, at least 80 Afghans have been moved to Louisiana from 34 other ICE facilities around the country, 19 of them without legal representation.
He said it was possible that there were hundreds of Afghans at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, which has served as a hub for ICE detainees before their deportation from the U.S.
If the U.S. sends Afghan detainees to Pakistan, they are not likely to be there long. Pakistan, which has hosted millions of Afghan refugees for decades, launched a sweeping crackdown in 2023, pressuring hundreds of thousands of Afghans to leave the country and forcibly deporting others.
They are arriving to an Afghanistan battered by multiple humanitarian crises, including widespread malnutrition , as well as an ongoing military conflict with neighboring Pakistan and a dramatic rollback of women’s rights under the Taliban’s hard-line Islamic policies.
VanDiver said the Trump administration would most likely be aware that Afghans sent to Pakistan would be at high risk of being returned to Afghanistan.
“You don’t have to be that smart to figure out that they’re sending them to Pakistan so that Pakistan will finish the job,” he said.
Regardless of whether they worked with the U.S. military, VanDiver said, any Afghans flown from the U.S. would be viewed with suspicion by the Taliban and at risk of persecution, imprisonment or worse.
That does not appear to be a major concern for the White House, said the senior administration official, who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
“The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.
VanDiver and others say the Trump administration’s treatment of Afghan allies could also have long-term consequences for U.S. national security by discouraging people in other countries from working with U.S. forces in future conflicts.
Asked whether the Trump administration was concerned about that, the official said, “I don’t think they care.”
The White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.” ICE did not respond to a request for comment.
A State Department spokesperson said the agency had “no plans to announce.”
“We reaffirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security and prosperity of their citizens,” the spokesperson said.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.
The senior administration official said the Afghans on the flight could include people with deportation orders, people who were turned down for asylum and people whose temporary protected status was terminated by the Trump administration. Many of the Afghans facing deportation requested asylum after crossing into the U.S. from Mexico, VanDiver said, and some of their cases are still pending.
Charlotte, a U.S. citizen whose Afghan husband has been in ICE detention since early 2025, said he had been moved to the Louisiana facility from Pennsylvania this month and told he would be deported in early November. She declined to be identified by her full name out of concern that her husband could be targeted by the Taliban.
Charlotte said she and her husband, whose asylum case has been pending for nine years, were visiting family in Maryland last year when he accidentally crossed into West Virginia and was pulled over. Though he was carrying his valid Illinois driver’s license, he did not have his work permit with him.
“When he was pulled over,” she said, “the sheriff actually said, ‘I’m an ICE agent. You’re going to immigration custody. I don’t care if the charges are dismissed, or I don’t care if you have a five-year work permit or Social Security card. I don’t care if you’re legal. Trump’s administration just took over — you’re going directly to immigration custody.’”
Charlotte sold their home in Illinois and moved to Maryland with their son, now 6, in order to be able to visit her husband at the ICE facility where he was held in Pennsylvania, about 100 miles away.
“I lost my nice house, our car, we left everything behind,” she said.
Over the next 20 months, when she took her son to see his father at the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, they were always separated by plexiglass.
“They never let him hug him one time,” Charlotte said. “We just sat there and cried every time.”
But at least they knew where he was and that he was OK, she said. Now that he’s in Louisiana, she said, “we can’t even visit or even say goodbye, he’s over 1,200 miles away.”
With her husband potentially being sent to Pakistan or Afghanistan — a country he hasn’t been to since 2016 — the uncertainty is even greater; Charlotte said he is growing his beard to comply with the Taliban’s strict rules for men’s facial hair.
“I’m just terrified that he’s not going to be safe,” she said, “or he’s going to be held in the jail and there’s nothing I can do.”
Charlotte said she believed her husband had been targeted for deportation because of a past conviction for a nonviolent crime that has since been resolved.
“I still don’t think this should end our entire life, for a child not to see his dad,” she said.
“He’s completely devastated and traumatized,” she said of their son. “He wants to fight. He wants to go protest. He wants to speak to Donald Trump. He basically knows so much more than he should.”

Ford's upcoming Fathom electric truck will be able to supply power to a home without a separate wall-mounted inverter when it launches in 2027, the automaker said Tuesday.
The Fathom, which will have a manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP) below $30,000, is expected to supply more than 10 kilowatts of AC power to a home. It will be the first EV from a U.S. automaker at that price point to offer the capability without a separate inverter, according to Ford.
The technology , which is known as bidirectional power, allows an EV's battery to send electricity back to a home or the electric grid.
FORD RECALLS MORE THAN 40,000 TRUCKS AND SUVS OVER VISIBILITY RISK
Ford's upcoming Fathom electric truck will be able to supply power to a home without a separate wall-mounted inverter when it launches in 2027. (Ford Motor Company)
Ford said cost has been a major obstacle to making bidirectional power more widely available because EVs have traditionally required additional equipment, like a separate inverter, to convert battery power for use in a home.
EV batteries store electricity as direct current (DC), while homes use alternating current (AC).
"That price tag has kept the technology in premium vehicles and the hands of early adopters," the automaker said. "Until now."
The Fathom will instead have an inverter built directly into the vehicle's E-box, taking away the need for a separate wall-mounted unit.
Customers will still need Ford's Home Power Station to use the truck's home power management feature, which allows owners to charge the Fathom when electricity is cheaper and use energy from its battery to power their home when electricity costs more.
"The only hardware required is Ford's Home Power Station, which is expected to cost about half as much as our first-generation bidirectional charger," the automaker said.
For backup power during an outage, customers will need both the home power station and Ford's home backup power panel. Ford said the required backup hardware is expected to cost at least 60% less than its first-generation home backup system.

A preproduction Ford Fathom electric truck drives past the "Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas" sign in Nevada.
Ford developed the system for its Universal EV Platform after acquiring startup Auto Motive Power in 2023.
"The system is simpler and more affordable, so more EV customers can have bidirectional power," Ford said.
The Fathom will be the first vehicle built on Ford's new Universal EV Platform. It will be assembled at the automaker's Louisville Assembly Plant, which is undergoing a $2 billion overhaul ahead of production in 2027.
Ford said utilities and regulators will also need to make it easier for bidirectional EVs to connect to the grid and participate in programs like virtual power plants.

A covered Ford Fathom moves through new production equipment at the Louisville Assembly Plant. (Ford Motor Company)
The automaker formed a working group with five major utilities in July to "help define scalable interconnection processes" ahead of Fathom's 2027 launch.

articles.title_orig: King to address slavery during Commonwealth speech in Antigua on final leg of Caribbean tour
articles.title_zh: King to address slavery during Commonwealth speech in Antigua on final leg of Caribbean tour
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.
The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.
It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
The King will make his speech at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.
"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."
When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to "the UK Government's position".
The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech where he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.
Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.
Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology are a matter for government, not the Palace.
"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to 'bat for Britain', the Realms and wider Commonwealth."
In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation" , and that Britain "must face up to the past".
His pledge to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by King Charles, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.
"Institutions are under strain across the globe," said a Palace spokesperson. "The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."
The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".
Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua, and they will attend a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island.
It has been a difficult few months for the King, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor , and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer.
In addition, his son the Duke of Sussex made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children in August.
Asked if the King was confident that his approach to family matters had been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. "Yes," a senior aide told the BBC. "That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done."
On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father , Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."
The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory".
In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

articles.title_orig: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
articles.title_zh: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
articles.content_orig:
Prime minister says shake-up is vital to restore tribunal crippled by years of political disputes
Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk , has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the country’s constitutional court, declaring that “in certain matters, there can be no compromise”.
In a prime-time television address on Saturday night , Tusk was defiant, despite overnight protests that saw riot police drafted to protect the court’s building, saying the shake-up was vital to restore a tribunal crippled by years of political disputes.
Paralysed for more than a decade, the court sat at the core of rule of law clashes between the rightwing Law and Justice (PiS) party and the EU during the party’s eight-year rule.
Since returning to office in 2023, the centre-right Tusk has sought to unwind those judicial changes , but his agenda has been frustrated by opposition-aligned presidents with extensive veto powers . Earlier this year, president Karol Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges approved by parliament.
The crisis flared again on Friday when a group of government-backed judges attempted to seize procedural control of the tribunal, suspending the PiS-appointed chief judge and deputy and prompting street protests.
Defending the action, Tusk said “there was never any doubt that the court in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court”, citing adverse rulings from European tribunals.
He compared the opposition outrage to “a thief snatching an elderly woman’s handbag, running off, and when he is caught, he screams that he is subjected to violence”.
Tusk said: “Let’s call things for what they are: for years, there have been organisations and politicians in Poland who seek to destroy democracy and the rule of law. It is no coincidence they find support among pro-Russian forces globally.”
He later highlighted that Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev had joined the opposition in an outcry over the changes, accusing Warsaw of “a constitutional coup” and “hounding the conservatives”. “And everything is clear,” Tusk said.
He also criticised opposition-aligned Nawrocki for joining the protests on Friday night and forcing his entry into the court’s building to intervene. “In a democratic state, no politician can enter a court to issue orders or intimidate judges – not even the president,” Tusk said. “We Poles have succeeded too well in building a strong state to surrender now.”
He said it was the government’s duty to ensure its security and the conditions necessary for the court to operate. “And I intend to fulfil that duty,” he said.

On Saturday, the European Commission urged Nawrocki to approve the new judges who were nominated by parliament, so the court could function in line with the constitution and EU law.
The confrontation sets the battle lines before next year’s parliamentary election, with polls pointing to a close race between Tusk’s broad coalition and the nationalist right.
However, experts remain divided over whether the government’s procedural gambit at the court is lawful.
Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights said on Saturday the legal basis for the temporary suspension was “questionable” , warning it would “not contribute” to restoring the court.
The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, conceded that the events outside the court were “not elegant” , but insisted: “The alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic.”
Nawrocki held some cross-party political talks on Saturday, with no apparent breakthrough. His senior aide, Zbigniew Bogucki, responded to Tusk’s address, calling the prime minister “a pathological liar, who is setting Poland ablaze”.

articles.title_orig: London police arrest 139 as hundreds protest Palestine Action ban
articles.title_zh: London police arrest 139 as hundreds protest Palestine Action ban
articles.content_orig:
London's Metropolitan Police arrested 139 people during a demonstration outside the US Embassy in the British capital on Saturday after protesters expressed support for Palestine Action , a pro-Palestinian group that has been outlawed in the UK and designated a terrorist organization.
The Metropolitan Police said most of those detained were arrested for expressing support for a banned organization and that officers continued making arrests at the scene.
According to a report by the Associated Press , many of the demonstrators were pensioners carrying signs reading, "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action." One protester also climbed a tree near the embassy and held up a sign calling for support for the organization.
The demonstration was organized by the activist group Defend Our Juries, which is campaigning against the British government's decision to outlaw Palestine Action.
According to the organizers, more than 4,000 people have been arrested since July 2025 for violating the ban on supporting the organization. The organizers condemned the arrests, arguing that detaining people for participating in peaceful demonstrations constituted a serious violation of civil rights and freedom of expression.
The British government banned Palestine Action in 2025 following a series of operations carried out by its members against defense facilities, particularly those belonging to Israeli defense company Elbit Systems .
Under British law, membership in or support for an organization designated as a terrorist group can carry a prison sentence of up to 14 years.
Palestine Action, founded in 2020, campaigns against what it describes as British military assistance to Israel. Its members say they seek to disrupt the operations of companies that support Israel's defense industry.
In 2024, activists from the organization broke into a British factory belonging to Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems and vandalized equipment using sledgehammers and crowbars.
In June 2025, activists broke into a British Royal Air Force base, sprayed red paint into the engines of two refueling aircraft, and caused additional damage using crowbars.
The US also took action against the organization, announcing sanctions against it in August and designating it a terrorist organization.
Alongside the London demonstration, a protest in support of Palestine Action was held outside the US Consulate in Edinburgh, Scotland.
No arrests were reported there, but Police Scotland announced that it was examining evidence to identify participants who wore shirts and carried signs expressing support for the banned organization. Police said further enforcement action could follow.
The demonstrations took place ahead of a hearing scheduled for Wednesday at the UK's Supreme Court, concerning an appeal against the authorities' decision to designate Palestine Action a terrorist organization.
Supporters of the group argue that the ban infringes on freedom of expression and the right to political protest.
